En 1480 et des poussières, alors que la princesse Blanche se prépare à épouser le beau prince du royaume voisin, son père décide de la marier à Melchior, son vulgaire chef des armées. C’est alors que sa marraine lui révèle être en possession d’une mystérieuse "peau" qui va permettre à Blanche, si elle la revêt, de devenir un homme, et ainsi de faire connaissance avec son fiancé incognito.

kopiëren", "links": [{"text": "Link kopiëren", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/het-zoekende-zelf-in-gesprek-met-taiyo-shimizu-larenas/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术家的名字有时就能勾起强烈的好奇心，就像一个人身上承载的不同语言那样。当我看到 Taiyo Shimizu Larenas 那奇特的画作时，这种好奇心愈发强烈。那是头骨、血淋淋的光头，还是一个正在休息的男人？在他在 De Ateliers 的工作室里，我们小心翼翼地交谈着。其中有沉默、长时间的深思，也有我们偶尔彼此心领神会的时刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Pelumi Adejumo", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我看到的你的画作，似乎脱离了某个固定的地点或身份。尽管如此，我还是想问问你是在哪里长大的，那种风景又是如何塑造你的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Taiyo Shimizu Larenas", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在荷兰出生，但在我很小的时候我们搬到了玻利维亚。我在那里住到两岁。随后我们在罗马住到四岁。接着我们回到了荷兰，并从荷兰去了美国。随后我们搬到了秘鲁。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的父母是外交官吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不是，他们从事发展援助工作。频繁的搬家对我的影响非常巨大。能看遍世界各地当然是一种特权。我一直对不同地方之间的巨大差异感到着迷。但与此同时这也是艰难的：作为孩子，不得不一次次重新建立友谊，却又不太理解为什么总得离开。我们从未在日本住过，我日本那边的家人都住在那里。我们每两三年会回去一次，但由于其间的时间跨度太大，我一直觉得跟家人保持着一种距离感。这也是一种完全不同的文化。我主要在西方文化中长大。我会说日语，但说得不是很好，因此也存在沟通的鸿沟。与此同时，那里一直充满着爱。这种规律性的搬家也带来了困惑。我认为这种长期的状态在我的作品中占据了主导地位。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种困惑是如何在你的作品中表现出来的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在美院时创作的作品带有一种存在主义的暗涌。我最初学的是摄影。我想吸引我的是因为它能够定格一个事件，它某种程度上是对记忆的一种替代。由于我们的生活总是在不断变动，记忆对我而言一直扮演着极其重要的角色。某样东西可能从一天到第二天就不再是我日常生活的一部分了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Left-behind-2026-1024x737.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Taiyo Shimizu Larenas - Left Behind (2026, 亚麻布油画, 140x200cm)", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Kabocha-2026-1024x827.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Taiyo Shimizu Larenas - Kabocha (2026, 亚麻布油画, 45x60cm)", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你是什么时候开始画画的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我学了三年摄影。但后来我觉得摄影过多地指向了外部现实，即世界本来的样子。我对内在世界更感兴趣，而绘画似乎能提供更直接的通往内在世界的途径。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不过我仍然把照片当作草图来用。我着迷于摄影那种难以捉摸的特质：捕捉某种氛围并在日后重返它的方式。为什么某种特定的物件、光线或心境会吸引我？我的作品非常关注氛围，而非具体的事物，恰恰相反，它关注的是模糊性。我仍在纠结摄影在我的创作实践中究竟扮演着什么角色。它仅仅是草图，还是照片本身也能独立存在？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在你早期的作品中，你非常关注人体的形象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，通常带着相当具有对抗性的目光。最近当我在 De Ateliers 内部换工作室时，我看到了我所有的旧作。一位女性朋友说：“它们都在看着我。”这是我刻意为之的。我想要创作出源于存在主义绝望的、直接且具有对抗性的图像，因为那时我的感受正是如此。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中也有沉睡的头像，散发着更多的平静。当时我觉得让我的作品探讨存在的宏大主题很重要。我深受存在主义文学的启发。如今回看，我理解那是当时的我所需要的，但我也看到了其中包含着多少自我怜悯。生活并非只有沉重的一面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我看来，这些作品也关乎关于身份与根基丧失的存在主义挣扎。是这样吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "恰恰相反。我尽量不给这些人物赋予太多辨识特征。这更像是一种尝试，试图创造一种抽象的人类，或者赋予灵魂和精神以某种形态。这些人物处于动荡之中，并不属于某个特定的地方。我有意识地以此营造一种情感强度，而不去讲一个具体的叙事。当时我在寻找一种普遍性。现在我绝对不认同这一点了。我是谁，怎么能由我来定义什么是普遍性？这终究是我自己的感受，是由一个非常西方的参照框架塑造的，其中包含着像弗朗西斯·培根（Francis Bacon）和米丽娅姆·卡恩（Miriam Cahn）这样的艺术家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我一眼就能看出这种渊源。粗犷的画面搭配抽象的人形，大量黑色与形成鲜明对比的亮色，以及许多暴力的表达。现在你换成了一种非常不同的风格。这种转变是如何产生的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我曾经固执地死守着一种创作形式。如果回头看，我会发现许多对同一个构想的变体。它与其说是通过绘画本身的探索，不如说是一种对某种情绪的图解。而后者正是我现在作品的发展方向。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Wasuregatami-2026-627x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Taiyo Shimizu Larenas - Wasuregatami (2026, 亚麻布油画, 110x200cm)", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Stoel-2026-1024x729.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Taiyo Shimizu Larenas - Stoel (2026, 亚麻布油画, 140x200cm)", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "许多画家终其一生都在寻找自己的个人风格。我觉得很厉害的是，你这么早就找到了。你会如何形容你现在的工作？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在以前的作品中陷入了死胡同，因为它们变得越来越重复。此外，我把自我的一部分与我所创作的东西以及我的创作方式紧密相连。当这些开始瓦解时，我不得不重新寻找。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在我的创作要开放得多。我不再是事先想要创作出一个画面，而是在寻找一个画面。因此，更多的层次感得以产生。我也不再画人形。物体和其他形态开始出现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管它们依然非常灰暗，但我看到了更多的静物，并且能感受到观察中的某种放缓。你能谈谈作品《Ie》里的那个房子吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那件作品是根据我当年在日本祖父母家附近拍的一张照片创作的。我奶奶去年去世了。她可能是我有幸认识的最特别的人。她是一个成长于某个时代和文化中的女性，在那个时代和文化中，她没法为自己做出太多的选择。尽管如此，她却充满了爱。我特别钦佩的是她的平静。我自己非常焦躁；我会丢东西，开始做一件事却不做完，或者无法完全专注于当下。而她则完全不同。她在对待事物时没有任何高低之分。洗碗、除草，她对待一切事物都带着同样的专注与爱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "人们对你新作品的反应与你的旧作品相比如何？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我还不太清楚，因为我几乎没有在这些工作室外面展出过它们。我的旧作品吸引了相当多忧郁的人，那些自身承载着某种痛苦的人。也许在我的作品中认出这种痛苦，给他们带来了一种平静。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也是为什么我觉得像培根（Bacon）这样的艺术家如此有趣。并不是因为我认出了某种具体的感受，而是因为我在作品中看到了自己。它让我觉得我并没有疯。这就是我觉得艺术特别的地方：各种体验可以在不同的形式中产生共鸣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我现在的作品可能依然是忧郁的。当我画完那些人物后不知道该画什么时，一位导师说了一句很重要的话：“你不需要非得通过人形来表达情感。你也可以让它从你观察事物的方式中自然流露。”我觉得这有趣得多：不是说“我现在要展示痛苦”，而是去探索一个画面是如何产生的。这为怀疑和改变留出了空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在有哪些艺术家、作家或音乐家对你很重要？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的音乐品味变了。我现在经常听米洛·J（Milo J）和卢奇奥·巴蒂斯蒂（Lucio Battisti）。在文学方面，我以前主要读陀思妥耶夫斯基。塞缪尔·贝克特的戏剧《等待戈多》我依然觉得很特别。对某种不会到来的东西无休止地等待，但同时又带有幽默感。你可以对着它又笑又哭。我最近读了奥尔加·托卡尔丘克的《白天的房子，夜晚的房子》，还有伊塔洛·卡尔维诺的《帕洛马尔》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Ik denk dat dat me aantrok omdat het een gebeurtenis vastlegt, het is een soort vervanging van een herinnering. Omdat ons leven telkens veranderde, hebben herinneringen voor mij altijd een grote rol gespeeld. Van de ene op de andere dag kon iets geen deel meer uitmaken van mijn dagelijks leven.

Wanneer begon je met schilderen?

Ik heb drie jaar fotografie gestudeerd. Op een gegeven moment vond ik dat dat te veel ging over een externe realiteit, met de wereld zoals die zich voordoet. Ik was meer geïnteresseerd in een innerlijke wereld en schilderen leek daar directer toegang toe te geven.

Wel gebruik ik nog steeds foto’s als schetsen. Ik vind het ongrijpbare van fotografie fascinerend: de manier waarop je een sfeer kunt vastleggen en er later op terug kunt komen. Waarom trok een bepaald object, licht of gemoedstoestand mij aan? Mijn werk gaat sterk over sfeer, niet over iets concreets, maar juist over ambiguïteit. Ik worstel nog met de vraag welke rol fotografie precies binnen mijn praktijk speelt. Is het een schets, of kan een foto ook op zichzelf staan?

In je oudere werk hield je je sterk bezig met het menselijk figuur.

Ja, vaak met vrij confronterende blikken. Toen ik onlangs binnen De Ateliers van studio verhuisde, zag ik al mijn oude werk weer. Een vriendin zei: “Ze kijken allemaal naar me.” Dat had ik doelbewust gedaan. Ik wilde directe, confronterende beelden maken die voortkwamen uit existentiële wanhoop, omdat ik me toen zo voelde.

Er waren ook slapende hoofden, die meer rust uitstraalden. Ik vond het destijds belangrijk dat mijn werk over grote thema’s van het bestaan ging. Ik was sterk geïnspireerd door existentiële literatuur. Als ik er nu naar kijk, begrijp ik dat het toen voor mij nodig was, maar ik zie ook hoeveel zelfmedelijden erin zat. Het leven is niet alleen maar zwaar.

Die werken gaan naar mijn idee ook over een existentiële worsteling met identiteit en ontworteling. Klopt dat?

Nee, juist niet. Ik probeerde de figuren zo min mogelijk identificatiekenmerken te geven. Het was eerder een poging om een soort geabstraheerde mens te maken, of een ziel of geest een vorm te geven. De figuren verkeerden in onrust en hoorden niet bij een specifieke plek. Ik wilde daarmee bewust een emotionele intensiteit creëren, zonder een concreet verhaal te vertellen. Destijds was ik op zoek naar een soort universaliteit. Nu ben ik het daar absoluut niet meer mee eens. Wie ben ik om te bepalen wat universeel is? Dat was uiteindelijk mijn eigen gevoel, gevormd vanuit een heel westers referentiekader, met kunstenaars als Francis Bacon en Miriam Cahn.

Ik zie de verwantschap meteen. Grove beelden met geabstraheerde mensfiguren, veel zwart en felle kleuren die een scherp contrast vormen en veel uitingen van geweld. Nu werk je in een heel andere stijl. Hoe ontstond die verandering?

Ik hield hardnekkig vast aan één vorm van werken. Als ik terugkijk, zie ik veel variaties op hetzelfde idee. Het was meer een illustratie van een gevoel dan een zoektocht door het schilderen zelf. Dat laatste is waar mijn werk nu naartoe gaat.

Er zijn veel schilders die hun hele leven op zoek zijn naar hun signatuur. Ik vind het juist knap dat je die zo vroeg hebt gevonden. Hoe zou je je huidige werk omschrijven?

Ik ben in mijn eerdere werk vastgelopen, omdat het steeds herhalender werd. Ik had bovendien een groot deel van mijn identiteit verbonden aan wat ik maakte en hoe ik dat maakte. Toen dat begon af te brokkelen, moest ik opnieuw zoeken.

Nu werk ik veel opener. In plaats van vooraf een beeld te willen maken, ben ik op zoek naar een beeld. Daardoor ontstaat meer gelaagdheid. Ik schilder ook geen menselijke figuren meer. Er verschijnen objecten en andere vormen.

Hoewel ze nog steeds erg grijs en grauw zijn, zie ik meer stillevens en voel ik een bepaalde vertraging in de observaties. Kun je iets vertellen over dat huis, in het werk Ie ?

Dat werk is gebaseerd op een foto die ik in de buurt van mijn grootouders in Japan heb gemaakt. Mijn oma is vorig jaar overleden. Zij was misschien wel de bijzonderste mens die ik ooit heb mogen kennen. Ze was een vrouw uit een generatie en cultuur waarin ze niet veel voor zichzelf kon kiezen. Toch was ze enorm liefdevol. Wat ik vooral bijzonder vind, is haar rust. Ik ben zelf heel rusteloos; ik raak dingen kwijt, begin iets en maak het niet af, of ben niet volledig aanwezig. Bij haar was dat totaal anders. Er was geen hiërarchie in hoe zij met dingen omging. De afwas, onkruid wieden, alles deed ze met dezelfde aandacht en liefde.

Hoe reageren mensen op je nieuwe werk in vergelijking met je oude werk?

Dat weet ik nog niet goed, omdat ik het nog nauwelijks buiten deze ateliers heb laten zien. Mijn oude werk trok vrij melancholische mensen aan, mensen die zelf een bepaalde pijn met zich meedroegen. Misschien gaf het herkennen van die pijn in mijn werk hen een soort rust.

Dat is ook waarom ik kunstenaars als Bacon zo interessant vond. Niet omdat ik een concreet gevoel herkende, maar omdat ik mezelf in het werk terugzag. Het gaf me het gevoel dat ik niet gek ben. Dat vind ik bijzonder aan kunst: ervaringen kunnen in verschillende vormen met elkaar rijmen.

Mijn huidige werk is misschien nog steeds melancholisch. Toen ik na de figuren niet meer wist wat ik moest schilderen, zei een tutor iets belangrijks: “Je hoeft gevoel niet per se uit te drukken in een menselijk figuur . Je kunt het ook laten ontstaan vanuit de manier waarop je naar iets kijkt.” Dat vind ik veel interessanter: niet zeggen “ik ga nu pijn laten zien” , maar onderzoeken hoe een beeld ontstaat. Dat geeft ruimte voor twijfel en verandering.

Zijn er kunstenaars, schrijvers of muzikanten die nu belangrijk voor je zijn?

Mijn muzieksmaak is veranderd. Ik luister nu veel naar Milo J en Lucio Battisti. Qua literatuur las ik vroeger vooral Dostojevski. Het toneelstuk Wachten op Godot van Samuel Beckett vind ik nog steeds bijzonder. Het eindeloze wachten op iets wat niet komt, maar tegelijkertijd met humor. Je kunt erom lachen en huilen. Onlangs heb ik Huis voor de dag, huis voor de nacht van Olga Tokarczuk gelezen. En Palomar van Italo Calvino.

Hoe kijk je naar het huidige kunstlandschap?

Het is makkelijk om principieel te zijn vanuit een geprivilegieerde positie. Ik zit nu bij De Ateliers, een geweldig instituut, en hoef me twee jaar geen zorgen te maken over inkomen, studioruimte of huisvesting. Dat is een enorm privilege.

Toch heb ik moeite met de manier waarop sociale media en de kunstwereld steeds meer met elkaar verweven zijn. Ik had ooit Instagram, maar ik merkte dat het platform mijn manier van kijken naar mijn eigen werk begon te beïnvloeden. Als ik meer likes kreeg, werd dat een vorm van validatie.

Sociale media bieden natuurlijk ook kansen. Tegelijkertijd lijkt de kunstwereld steeds transactioneler te worden: wie kent wie, wie volgt wie, wie stuurt wie een DM ? Dat staat voor mij haaks op waar kunst over gaat. We leven in een digitale, kapitalistische samenleving waarin efficiëntie centraal staat, terwijl kunst juist interessant is omdat ze niet efficiënt of pragmatisch hoeft te zijn. Kunst werkt subtieler en is niet altijd concreet.

Ik zie ook een soort fetisjisme rond ‘jong’ en ‘nieuw’. Er moet voortdurend iets nieuws komen. Sommige kunstenaars lijken steeds hetzelfde werk te produceren, waardoor je een productiemachine wordt in plaats van dat je blijft zoeken.

Natuurlijk verschilt dat per kunstenaar. Een kleine verschuiving in materiaal of kleur kan al heel experimenteel voelen. Maar ik heb het idee dat er soms iets van de ziel uit het werk wordt getrokken, doordat we ons allemaal aanpassen aan dat systeem.

Tegelijkertijd moet ik voorzichtig zijn met die kritiek. Het is makkelijk om daar nu een mening over te hebben, omdat ik het op dit moment niet nodig heb. Misschien verandert dat ooit. Maar voorlopig wil ik vooral blijven zoeken.

Over de Buning Brongers Prijzen De Buning Brongers Prijs is een Nederlandse kunstprijs voor jonge beeldend kunstenaars. De prijzen worden eens in de twee jaar uitgereikt door de Buning Brongers Stichting uit de nalatenschap van Johan Buning en zijn familie. De prijs bestaat dit jaar 60 jaar en is sinds 1966 uitgereikt aan 174 kunstenaars. Aan de prijs is een geldbedrag verbonden van € 4.500 per winnaar. De kandidaten voor de prijs zijn de afgelopen twee jaar afgestudeerd aan kunstacademies in Nederland en voorgedragen door hun academie. De prijsuitreiking en opening van de tentoonstelling van de zes winnaars vinden plaats op vrijdag 13 november in Arti et Amicitiae te Amsterdam. Je bent van harte uitgenodigd hierbij aanwezig te zijn.

Een gesprek over kunst en kwaliteit in Spui 25 Voorafgaand aan de prijsuitreiking in Arti et Amicitiae organiseert de stichting een gesprek over kunst en kwaliteit in Spui 25. Hans den Hartog Jager en Heske ten Cate geven elk een presentatie waarin ze dieper ingaan op hun persoonlijke ervaringen en inzichten. Aansluitend gaan Dineke Blom, Ricardo van Eyk en Robert Zandvliet met elkaar in gesprek. Je bent ook hier van harte welkom!

article_text:
F or a film that dispenses a lot of backstory information via intertitles, you are left with a lot of questions when the credits finally roll. For example, how in the world did Irish film-maker Sinéad O’Shea gain access to her main subject: James Cox Chambers, AKA “Fergie”, the American heir to a multimillion-dollar fortune – whom we first meet as the founding member and bankroller of a communist community of less than a dozen people in Alford, a town in rural Massachusetts. A scion of the wealthy Cox family, a liberal clan who have backed leftist causes in the past, Fergie wants to take things even further politically and is willing to use his own hefty inheritance (about $250m) to support his fellow communards’ commitment to learning, self-sustaining farm work and running a jujitsu studio and gym that won’t accept members of the police as members.

But when the group decide to protest at Elbit Systems, the Israeli-owned arms manufacturer, its actions slide into “criminal mischief and criminal trespassing”, according to reports. Several Alford members are arrested, including one Paige Belanger; O’Shea’s film cuts back and forth between interviews with Belanger and other communards and Chambers, who has scarpered to Tunisia. Although he pays for Belanger’s defence and covers other costs arising from the action, considerable rancour rises between Fergie, Paige and other former Alford community members, that O’Shea perhaps wisely doesn’t let the film get too bogged down with trying to parse.

Nevertheless, O’Shea’s admirable attempt to not take sides leaves a muddle of sorts at the centre of the story, making it unclear who or what is the real subject of the film. We are left with a messy tangle of historical fact, colourful personalities and dramatic biographies that could have made a longer film. But any way you slice it, Fergie – whose extradition to the US from Spain is being sought over his alleged support for Hamas – comes across as a compellingly weird character, a confused soul who covers himself in tattoos, discourse and delusions to hide a considerable amount of pain stemming from a traumatic adolescence. Sure, it would be easy to sneer at him and say poor little rich boy, but there’s something about his struggle for authenticity that feels timely and significant in these complex times.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Disney and NBCUniversal accused Midjourney of being a “bottomless pit of plagiarism” in a lawsuit last year . More than 18 months on, the company allegedly has failed to clean up its act.

VN. ai , a tech startup that stress tests generative artificial intelligence tools for copyright infringement, has produced its first quarterly report examining how 15 popular AI models performed when it comes to flouting studio IP.

Related Stories

YouTuber Gossip Goblin Releases Trailer For R-Rated AI Theatrical Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’

The research conducted last month found that Midjourney v8.1 was the worst offender when it came to reproducing images of copyrighted characters. The AI model also outranked competitors on so-called “brand safety violations,” meaning characters were placed in a “harmful context,” such as scenes of violence or drug taking.

RELATED: Sora Is Coming, Sora Is Here, And Hollywood Is Sore

Watch on Deadline

According to VN.ai’s report, which was shared with Deadline, Midjourney reproduced images of characters that violated brand safety measures once in every three text prompts, or 37% of the time. This included a Midjourney v8.1 hallucination in which it generated an image of The Joker smoking cannabis while wearing a dress that could have been ripped from the wardrobe of Frozen’s Elsa.

Midjourney did not respond to requests for comment. Disney and NBCUniversal’s lawsuit against the company remains ongoing, and Warner Bros Discovery also has filed suit . The startup has argued that training its AI models on images of copyrighted material is permitted under fair use.

VN.ai’s report found that every AI model generated at least one copyright-protected character, even when a character’s name was not referenced in a text prompt. This included Google’s Nano Banana and ByteDance’s model Seedance 2.5, though the latter has improved significantly after receiving cease-and-desist letters from Hollywood studios.

As noted recently by Deadline, other Chinese AI models continue to plunder IP , including MiniMax H3, which generated videos that violated studio brand safety standards 55% of the time when an image was used in a prompt.

Asked why AI models continue to flout copyright, VN.ai founder Nelson Chu said it was “good for business.” He added: “It’s great marketing. It works. It gets people to use your model and pay for it.”

Chu predicts change, however. “I do think at some point that’s just not going to be OK. And I think as more models set the precedent for how it is to be a good actor here, you will see more improvement,” he told Deadline.

article_text:
The International Film Festival Rotterdam ( IFFR ) has unveiled a first selection of 10 feature titles locked to world premiere in the Bright Future and Harbour sidebars of its 56th edition in early 2027.

The Harbour sidebar, inspired by Rotterdam ’s port city identity and “offering a safe haven” to contemporary filmmakers pushing cinematic boundaries, welcomes back a trio of directors with IFFR connections.

Angolan director Kiluanji Kia Henda, who previously attended with Short Profile in 2020 and commissioned performance Resetting Birds’ Memories in 2021, returns with Karl Marx, Luanda (scroll down for synopses)

Related Stories

Cypriot filmmaker Kyros Papavassiliou returns with Yiannis, following his 2015 IFFR Tiger Competition selection for Impressions of a Drowned Man . Additionally, Hong Kong director Rita Hui Nga Shu is back, following the premiere of Decameron in 2021, with The Lapse .

Watch on Deadline

IFFR newcomers in the Harbour selection include Malaysian filmmaker siblings Iskander and Feisal Azizuddin with comedy cannibal horror Ali and Ben’s Spicy Meats , and Omer Shamir with intimate docu-portrait Waiting Room .

First titles for Bright Future, focused on emerging talents, Ben Hicks’s Kids Go Free made over 15 years across three countries; director Parbat Chapagai’s stylised Dostoevsky adaptation Portrait of a Young Criminal , Lucila Las Heras’s dark fairy tale The Muglur , Mohamed El Zayat’s ensemble dramedy In The Name of Galeela and Ali Bakhtiari documentary Tehran The Obscure Atelier of Desire .

“These first ten films already offer a glimpse of that incredible range, from the playful and provocative to the intimate and politically urgent,” said Vanja Kaludjercic, Festival Director at IFFR. “Cinema is at its most exciting when it challenges our expectations, when filmmakers find new ways to express experiences, contradictions and realities that resist easy answers.”

Alongside the first film announcements, IFFR also unveiled its 2027 festival campaign, developed in collaboration with Rotterdam design studio 75B and echoing IFFR’s interest in artists finding new forms to express the experience of the world around them

“We wanted our campaign for 2027 to reflect that same spirit of artistic freedom and curiosity. A reminder that there is no single way of looking at the world, and that there is always more to discover in how others see it,” said Kaludjercic.

Previous titles in Bright Future from IFFR’s 2026 edition include: Ah Girl (IFFR’s Youth Jury Award and TIFF 2026), Let Them Be Seen (BFI London Film Festival 2026), while notable 2026 Harbourt titles include James J. Robinson’s debut First Light, Australia’s Academy Award Entry for Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards in 2027.

IFFR’s 56th edition will run from January 28 to February 7 2027. The complete lineup will be unveiled on 16 December 2026.

Details of the first selections (synopses provided by IFFR)

BRIGHT FUTURE

THE MUGLUR Director: Lucila Las Heras Mexico, Argentina Struggling to write a fantasy novel under the thumb of her alcoholic father, Aurora makes a Faustian bargain with a strange creature: the Muglur. But what price will it ask of her? The answer will be found at the dark heart of this claustrophobic fairy tale.

IN THE NAME OF GALEELA Director: Mohamed El Zayat Egypt When money for a pilgrimage to Mecca is stolen, a young man’s community comes together to convince his blind grandmother that she’s still going. Egyptian filmmaker Mohamed El Zayat asks us how far we’ll go for someone we love in his endlessly creative debut feature.

KIDS GO FREE United States, Taiwan, Japan A taste for worldly adventures can bring passionate love and the thrill of the unknown, as well as niggling questions about economic security and one’s future. Told through a kaleidoscopic structure and a humanist lens over 15 years, Ben Hicks’ debut feature tackles these concerns in a miraculous manner.

PORTRAIT OF A YOUNG CRIMINAL Director: Parbat Chapagai United States, Nepal David, a destitute tutor, develops an attachment to teenage sex worker Sonya. Wishing to save her from the spiritual squalor of their surroundings, David resolves to kill his rich employer. A stark, psychologically vivid adaptation of Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment set in small-town Nepal.

HARBOUR

KARL MARX, LUANDA Director: Kiluanji Kia Henda Angola, Portugal Kiluanji Kia Henda’s satirical future history of Angola imagines that the nation renews itself as a Marxist state. Via time-travelling love story and bold Afro-sci-fi-spaghetti-Western, we are reminded of a rare basic truth: in the forest, political doctrines do not help the rain fall.

ALI AND BEN’S SPICY MEATS Director: Feisal Azizuddin, Iskander Azizuddin Malaysia Ali and Ben, broke buddies running a failing pickle business, stumble upon a magic recipe made from human meat. When their overnight success attracts the suspicion of a local politician, the friends must do what it takes to protect their nascent empire in this zany horror-comedy.

WAITING ROOM (World Premiere) Director: Omer Shamir France Fleeing from Khan Younis, award-winning Palestinian photojournalist Mohammed Zaanoun moves his immediate family to safety in Egypt, unsure of what’s to come. Filmmaker and activist Omer Shamir paints a moving documentary portrait of this family, in their exile home, across one year.

THE LAPSE (World Premiere) Director: Rita Hui Nga Shu Taiwan, United Kingdom Hong Kong filmmaker and artist Rita Hui Nga Shu layers life, declassified governmental documents and her AI-cloned voice to open a dialogue between the promises on paper and the reality of life for Hong Kongers. An uncompromising, impactful and radically human film-essay.

TEHRAN THE OBSCURE ATELIER OF DESIRE (World Premiere) Director: Ali Bakhtiari Iran A contemporary documentary portrait of artists in their studios across Tehran. They return to unfinished canvases, abandoned experiments and sketches of future projects. They scrape, paint, sculpt and listen intently to music, while outside, the threat of war looms.

YIANNIS (World Premiere) Director: Kyros Papavassiliou Cyprus, Greece When his father’s body vanishes from the morgue, a Cypriot teenager and his mother cross into the occupied north to find Yiannis, a bird psychologist from his father’s past. Kyros Papavassiliou turns a missing-body mystery into a dreamlike journey through grief on a divided island rarely seen on screen.

article_text:
A Canadian seafood tycoon’s financial troubles have turned into a debate over who gets to decide what happens to his art collection, which includes dozens of Indigenous artifacts that some experts say should be returned to their communities of origin.

John Risley, the billionaire businessman who cofounded Clearwater Seafoods, is caught up in a dispute over hundreds of artworks and antiques following the collapse of his investment company, CFFI Ventures, which entered creditor protection in March with nearly $1 billion in debt.

Among the objects ensnared in the proceedings are roughly 30 Indigenous artifacts, including baskets, moccasins, textiles, and bone carvings. According to the Canadian Press outlet CBC , which first reported the concerns, some are attributed to Inuit, Mi’kmaq, or Cree makers, while others have the vague identifier “Indigenous” and no listed artist or date.

That lack of information has prompted calls from repatriation experts for Indigenous communities to be consulted before the objects change hands.

Cody Groat, a history and Indigenous studies professor at Western University, told the Canadian Press that the dispute raises broader questions about when Indigenous nations should have a say in the sale of objects associated with their cultural heritage. He believes the best outcome would be for culturally significant objects to be returned to their communities.

Risley, however, disputes the idea that his collection contains objects that should to be repatriated.

He told the Canadian Press that he supports repatriation in principle but believes his acquisitions were made through reputable dealers and auction houses, where culturally sensitive material would already have attracted scrutiny.

“Our collection would not include any such pieces,” he said, adding that dealers and auction houses have little interest in handling objects that might raise repatriation concerns.

The Canadian Museums Association ‘s Indigenous Council disagrees with his reasoning. In a statement to the Canadian Press, the council argued that Indigenous communities themselves are best equipped to determine the cultural importance of such objects, rather than collectors, dealers, or museums.

The spat comes as Risley’s creditors attempt to recover money from the collapse of CFFI Ventures.

In September, a Nova Scotia court approved the transfer of most of the company’s assets to New Tide Capital, an affiliate of New York–based HPS Investment Partners, which held most of CFFI’s debt.

The assets included a collection of more than 1,200 artworks and antiques valued at approximately $8.1 million. Among them were more than 95 paintings by Canadian folk artist Maud Lewis, works by members of the Group of Seven, and pieces by Inuit artists Jessie Oonark and Irene Avaalaaqiaq Tiktaalaaq.

But the ownership of 669 objects became a separate point of contention. Risley maintains that those works belong to him personally rather than to his company. A lawyer for New Tide told the court that the firm would seek to resolve the dispute privately.

The Indigenous artifacts appear on that disputed list.

Canada has no comprehensive legal framework governing the repatriation of Indigenous cultural objects, and private collections present particular challenges. Unlike museums, which often face pressure to disclose their holdings and investigate provenance, private collectors generally aren’t under a similar obligation.

Lauren Wheeler, executive director of the Canadian Museums Association, told the CBC that the limited information available about Risley’s holdings illustrates how hard it can be to identify culturally significant objects in private hands.

The association has developed guidance encouraging museums to work with Indigenous communities to identify and return objects acquired through coercion, forced displacement, or other questionable circumstances. Wheeler thinks private collectors should follow similar practices.

Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, a national organization representing the Inuit in Canada, has also offered to help examine any potentially significant Inuit objects in the collection and facilitate their return where appropriate.

For now, there’s no proof that the Indigenous artifacts in Risley’s collection were improperly acquired, nor has a specific community established a claim to any of the objects identified in the court proceedings.

article_text:
After two years of research, the spot where two strangers stood—believed to be the first human beings ever captured in a photograph—has been identified. It will be marked with a permanent plaque on October 15, 2026, at Place de la République in Paris.

One spring morning in 1838, the inventor Louis Daguerre leans out of the window of his studio and points his camera at the view before him. On the Boulevard du Temple, it is rush hour. But the exposure, lasting several minutes, cannot capture the bustle of Paris.

When the image appears on the silvered plate, Daguerre discovers an unforeseen detail: a bootblack and his customer who, by chance, stayed still long enough. These two strangers are believed to be the first human beings ever to appear in a photograph.

“The presence of these two figures is entirely down to chance. Neither the bootblack nor his customer was posing for the camera: it is a kind of photobomb before its time. That is also what is wonderful about photography. It retains what was there, in front of the lens, at a precise moment.”

— Axel Danielson, director and producer

The spot where they stood that morning had never been identified, let alone marked. On October 15, 2026, that will change.

A PERMANENT PLAQUE IN THE HEART OF PARIS

Un Détail Imprévu is a bronze plaque that will be set into the paving of the Place de la République, at the spot where the bootblack and his customer stood in 1838—within the present-day boundaries of the square, in line with the Rue du Faubourg-du-Temple. It is the culmination of two years of research by the filmmakers and producers Kalle Boman, Axel Danielson, and Maximilien Van Aertryck, with the support of the City of Paris for its permanent installation in public space.

Designed and produced by the team, the plaque measures 68 × 95 cm and reproduces a detail of Daguerre’s image, accompanied by a text telling its story. The project is supported by the City of Paris, notably its Direction des affaires culturelles, and has been awarded the Bicentenaire de la Photographie label by the French Ministry of Culture.

THE RESEARCH: FINDING THE SPOT

Between June 2024 and April 2026, the team assembled a cross-referenced body of data: a complete 3D scan of the Place de la République and the Boulevard du Temple, a survey of Paris archives (engravings, cadastral plans, early nineteenth-century paintings), and a reconstruction of the neighborhood as it was before the square was created.

This data was then entrusted to two architecture firms, the Swedish Rumlab and the French Mater Studio, which each located the spot independently, using different methods. Three of the buildings visible in Daguerre’s image still exist today and served as essential reference points for the calculation.

As it is most often reproduced, Daguerre’s image is in fact flipped horizontally—a consequence of the camera obscura principle, in which light projects the inverted scene onto the back of the box.

“What fascinates us is that the first photograph of human beings shows a social relationship: a bootblack, probably a child, and his customer, an adult.”

— Maximilien Van Aertryck, director and producer

The search for this spot is part of a broader inquiry into the early days of photography, which the team hopes to continue in the form of an exhibition and a book.

A TRIAL

The image of the Boulevard du Temple belongs to a series of trials. Daguerre photographed the same view from his window at different times of day. He titled this one “Huit heures du matin” (eight in the morning).

In 1822, Daguerre opened the Diorama in Paris, a theater where vast painted canvases were transformed before the audience’s eyes through effects of light. His home and studio adjoined the hall. It was there that, from 1829, he pursued his research with Nicéphore Niépce, and then alone after Niépce’s death in 1833. It led, in 1837, to the perfection of the daguerreotype, the first photographic process to spread across the entire world.

Nearly two centuries later, this story resonates with another upheaval in our relationship to images.

THE TITLE: “UN DÉTAIL IMPRÉVU”

“When France gave Daguerre’s invention to the world, no one yet knew what it would be used for. François Arago, the politician and scientist, gave a speech in which he affirmed that it was above all the unforeseen that one should count on. We think photography is a wonderful instrument for discovering the world precisely because it records more than the person holding the camera intended. That is where the plaque’s title comes from: Un Détail Imprévu.”

— Maximilien Van Aertryck

FIRST REACTIONS, 1839

In 1838, when the image was made, what Daguerre was doing had no name yet. Barely a handful of people knew what he was working on in his studio. It would take until the summer of 1839 for the French state to acquire the process and give it to the entire world.

“When Daguerre made this image, there was not really a name yet for what he was doing. In his correspondence with Niépce, you can see them searching for a way to name the invention. They write that nature itself leaves an imprint, that it writes its own image, without any human hand intervening.”

— Kalle Boman

In March 1839, Samuel Morse was in Paris to present his telegraph. He asked to meet Daguerre, and the two men demonstrated their inventions to each other. Morse, himself a painter and portraitist, examined Daguerre’s plates through a magnifying glass and wrote that the interior views were “Rembrandt perfected.” In a letter to his brother, he described the bootblack and his customer: the only human beings visible on a boulevard otherwise full of people. The letter was subsequently widely reprinted in the American press.

“The reactions of the time capture the shock that the invention of photography represented. ‘It’s nature itself!’ ‘Is it art or science?’ ‘It’s too beautiful to be true.’ And then there are the art critics, who reproached it in particular for its attention to details deemed useless or anecdotal.”

— Axel Danielson

THE ORIGINAL TODAY

In October 1839, Daguerre sent several of his plates to the sovereigns of Europe. The one showing the bootblack and his customer went to Ludwig I of Bavaria and joined the collections of the Bavarian National Museum in Munich.

The plate was severely damaged during the Second World War. In the 1970s, an unfortunate restoration attempt erased the image almost entirely. Today, only a few faint traces remain. A photograph made in 1936 is the only known reproduction from before the image disappeared. The negative of that photograph has also been lost.

WHY NOW: THE BIRTH OF PHOTOGRAPHY IN THE AGE OF AI

There are now more cameras on Earth than pairs of eyes. Yet among the images that surround us, a growing number were taken by no camera at all.

“We stand at the crossroads of photography and promptography—that is, AI-generated imagery. In photography, what you see was necessarily there: it takes light, reflected by something real, entering the camera. To appear on Daguerre’s plate, these two people had to be there, at that spot, at that hour. Today, we can fabricate images of people who never existed. That is also why it seems important to us to mark this place.”

— Kalle Boman

“The plaque is a reminder that earlier generations were confronted, as we are today, with the arrival of a new technology and the need to understand and manage its consequences.”

— Kalle Boman, producer

THE TEAM BEHIND THE PROJECT

Un Détail Imprévu is a project by Kalle Boman, Axel Danielson, and Maximilien Van Aertryck, carried by the company Mandé.

Maximilien Van Aertryck and Axel Danielson

Maximilien Van Aertryck (born 1989 in Livry-Gargan, French-German-Swedish) and Axel Danielson (born 1976 in Vittskövle, Sweden) are directors and producers, partners at Plattform Produktion. They have worked together since 2013, developing a documentary cinema concerned in particular with how images shape our perception of the world and our behavior.

Their short film Ten Meter Tower (2016), viewed several million times online, is one of the most-watched Op-Docs in the history of The New York Times . Shortlisted for the Oscars and nominated for the Emmy Awards, it entered the permanent collection of Finland’s Museum of Modern Art, KIASMA.

In 2023, they directed What a Fantastic Machine , a feature-length documentary on two centuries of image culture, from the camera obscura to social media. The film won the Special Jury Award for Creative Vision at Sundance and two awards at the Berlinale, before being distributed in more than thirty countries. It also gave rise to an image-literacy campaign followed by more than 30,000 students in Sweden, Germany, and France.

Their latest film, Death of a Fantastic Machine (2025), published by The New York Times Op-Docs, continues their reflection on our relationship to images.

Kalle Boman

Born in 1943 in Stockholm, Kalle Boman is a film producer, creative consultant, and professor. Active in cinema since 1964, he has collaborated notably with Bo Widerberg, Roy Andersson, Marie-Louise Ekman, and Ruben Östlund. He received the Honorary Guldbagge in 2014 for his lifetime achievement and has taught since 2009 in the film department of the University of Gothenburg (HDK-Valand).

Mandé

Founded in Paris in 2026 by Maximilien Van Aertryck and Axel Danielson, Mandé works in visual creation and image and media education. Un Détail Imprévu is its first production.

Plattform Produktion

Founded in Gothenburg in 2002 by the producer Erik Hemmendorff and the director Ruben Östlund, Plattform Produktion has produced all of Ruben Östlund’s films, including The Square (2017) and Triangle of Sadness (2022), both Palme d’Or winners at Cannes and Oscar-nominated. Since its founding, the company has received four Oscar nominations, won eight European Film Awards, and earned more than one hundred international prizes.

SUPPORTERS

The project is supported by the Hasselblad Foundation, the City of Paris (Direction des affaires culturelles), Visuellt Center and the Region of Jönköping, Lion Hill Production, and Konstnärsnämnden (Swedish Arts Grants Committee).

The project is produced by Mandé in collaboration with Plattform Produktion, and has received the Bicentenaire de la Photographie label from the French Ministry of Culture. The City of Paris supports the realization of the project and its permanent installation at Place de la République.

PRACTICAL INFORMATION Unveiling date: October 15, 2026 Location: Place de la République, Paris Time: 4:45 p.m.

Films and events

Cult

The Face of Horror

In this stunning, blood-soaked homage to Technicolor horror films, a woman in medieval England rises from the grave to wreak revenge on her husband.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Anna Biller

With Jonah Hauer-King, Kristine Froseth, Ellie Bamber

UK 2026. 120min

Courtesy of Embankment Films

Language English

Introduction

Returning as a ghost after a cruel betrayal results in her death, Eleanor and her sister deliver bloody vengeance on the man who took her life and murdered their father. Anna Biller, writer-director of The Love Witch, here delivers a rich visual feast. Gloriously shot on 35mm, this supernatural Gothic melodrama vibrantly brings 14th-century England to life.

Victoria Millington

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury, self-harm, and sexual violence.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The Blood Countess

Isabelle Huppert dazzles as the Blood Countess in this delightful and high-camp gothic fantasy from visionary filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger.

Nightborn

A couple’s dream of idyllic family life in the Finnish woods is shattered by the arrival of their nightmarish new baby, in Hanna Bergholm’s riotously gory folk horror.

Rogue Trooper

Duncan Jones brings the beloved 2000 AD comic strip to life with an all-guns-blazing sci-fi animation, about a soldier in a dystopian future who is sent on an impossible mission.

article_text:
“Deadstream” helmers Joseph and Vanessa Winter are set to direct horror-thriller “Future Me,” based on a viral Reddit short story by Daria Vasileva. The film is the first title of a multi-picture deal between L.A. and UAE-based production company Longevity Pictures , indie genre label Spooky Pictures and Abu Dhabi’s Image Nation Studios.

Originally published in the “NoSleep” subreddit — the online community dedicated to user-generated horror fiction — “Future Me” follows a man “who receives a deeply unsettling email from his past self via the ‘FutureMe’ website, a message that draws him down a terrifying and increasingly surreal rabbit hole,” according to its synopsis.

Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: 'I Know That We Could Do Better'

“Deadstream” was the first feature by the husband-and-wife filmmaking team. The horror comedy premiered at SXSW in 2022 before being acquired by Shudder, where it became one of the genre streaming platform’s most acclaimed original releases. They followed that success by directing the fan-favorite segment “To Hell and Back” in found-footage horror anthology film “V/H/S/99.”

Joseph and Vanessa Winter’s next project is the previously announced film “Amityville,” a radical new spin on the Amityville horror franchise that is being produced by Adam Hendricks and Greg Gilreath of Divide/Conquer and Raphael Margules and J.D. Lifshitz, principals of genre-focused production label BoulderLight Pictures.

Joseph and Vanessa Winter’s upcoming “Future Me” will instead be produced by Majd Nassif (“Mercy”) for Longevity Pictures, alongside Steven Schneider (“Late Night With the Devil”) and Roy Lee (“Weapons,” “Barbarian”) for Spooky Pictures. Image Nation Studios’ Ben Ross (“Watcher,” “Late Night With the Devil”) and Longevity Pictures’ Aysel Lyatifova, (“Six Till Midnight”) will executive produce.

“Future Me” follows the initial collaboration between Longevity Pictures, Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Studios on upcoming horror thriller “Home Safety Hotline” directed by Michael Matthews (“Love and Monsters”) and based on Night Signal Entertainment’s popular puzzle video game of the same name. Other titles on their multi-picture slate remain to be unveiled.

The Winters are represented by WME, TFC Management, and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, and Rush & Kaller, L.L.P.

“Spooky Pictures and Image Nation Studios have built an incredible track record for championing high-concept, creator-driven horror storytelling, so expanding our partnership felt like a natural next step,” Nassif said in a statement.

“After the success of ‘Backrooms,’ the potential of internet lore as fertile ground for adaptation has become undeniable,” he went on to note. “So we’re excited to be bringing ‘Future Me’ to life with a team which shares our passion for original and punchy genre projects.”

Commented Spooky Pictures’ Steven Schneider and Image Nation Studios’ Ben Ross: “Longevity Pictures brings exactly the kind of creative flair and commercial instinct that we champion, so we’re thrilled to be building a slate together that combines killer storytelling with strong commercial appeal.”

“Horror filmmaking is firing on all cylinders right now, with both audiences and critics embracing fresh concepts and emerging creative voices, making this the ideal time to bring more genre films to audiences worldwide,” they added. “‘Future Me” is exactly the kind of project we’re looking to get behind — a chilling premise with a passionate existing fanbase, and with Joseph and Vanessa Winter on board, it has all the makings of a standout horror film.”

ホワイトハウスが「まるで独裁者のファミレス」──オバマ元大統領がトランプの「金ピカ改装」を揶揄

アメリカ 中間選挙の投開票日が11月3日に迫り、各地で舌戦が繰り広げられている。そんな中、 トランプ 大統領が進めようとしているホワイトハウスの大改修に、オバマ、クリントン両元大統領が相次いで苦言を呈した。

10月23日、ホワイトハウスのダン・スカビーノ次席補佐官が、 ドナルド・トランプ 大統領が計画しているボールルーム（宴会場）建設現場の空撮動画をX（旧ツイッター）に 投稿 した。これを受け、24日にオハイオ州で開かれた集会に出席したバラク・オバマ元大統領は、動画に関する自身の見解を次のように述べている。

「お気づきかもしれませんが、彼は住宅の改装に非常に熱心なようです。HGTV（家探しや劇的リノベーションなどのリアリティーショーを放映）に出るべきですね」

さらに、「ホワイトハウスの本館よりも大きな宴会場」が建設されようとしていることに触れ、「あの金ピカづくしはどういうことなのでしょう？ ホワイトハウスの見た目が、まるでサダム・フセイン元イラク大統領がザ・チーズケーキ・ファクトリー（米ファミリーレストランチェーン）をオープンしたかのようになってしまっています」と語りかけた。

トランプ大統領がこだわる豪華な内装への批判はこれだけではない。23日に フロリダ州 ハリウッドで行われた応援演説で、ビル・クリントン元大統領もホワイトハウスの改装工事を揶揄。庭園の芝生を石造りのパティオに敷き替え、 アメリカ 建国の父たちの彫刻を設置したことについて、「ローズガーデンを、まるでリベラーチェのバスルームの入り口のようにしてしまうことに議会が抗議しなかったのは間違いだったと思う」と述べた（リベラーチェは金銀の総ラメなど派手な衣装で人気を博した20世紀のピアニスト）。

米連邦最高裁は8月31日、トランプ政権がホワイトハウスの東棟（イーストウィング）を解体した後に進めようとしている宴会場建設工事の継続を承認。巨額の費用を投じるこの計画について、賛成5、反対4で、地上部分の建設を差し止めた下級審の判決が覆えされた。

最高裁は、議会によって設立された非営利団体「全米歴史保存トラスト」の関係者は、当該プロジェクトによって直接的な被害を受けないため、同団体には訴訟を提起する法的根拠がないとの判断を示している。同団体は昨年、建設計画に関する連邦議会の承認を得ないままホワイトハウスの東棟を取り壊したトランプ政権を提訴していた。最高裁判決が出た際、同トラストのブレント・レッグス会長はこう述べている。

「これは、我々の訴訟の核心部分に関する最終的な決定ではなく、各代の大統領は『国民の家（ホワイトハウス）』の一時的な管理者に過ぎず、議会の承認なしにそれを解体・再設計する一方的な権限はないという根本的な論点を解決するものでもありません」（翻訳：石井佳子）

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "蒂埃里·曼德罗的每月沉思", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我将引导你们的思考转向一个时事性的话题，它非常适合现在正涌现的迷雾（无论秋令还是春令，取决于你所在的半球）。我出于谦逊才说迷雾，因为有时我们会遇到足以遮蔽最敏锐、最宽容双眼的浓雾。借鉴法律和文学的各种定义，我们可以大体将“歧视”理解为：由于某人或某物属于不同的社群或生活方式而对其进行排斥。所有这些在交往标准上如此不同的社群遭到排斥，在所谓的集体社会生活中普遍被法律所禁止，且完全无法辩解。因肤色、私生活、哲学参考或宗派观点而将个人排斥在社会之外，是绝对应受谴责的。然而事实依然是，脑力、身体潜能、感官财富的平等并不存在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如常有的那样，当今的问题诞生于混淆。对渴望与现实之间的一种粗暴混杂，将我们引入了一个彻底的死胡同，损害了创造力和能力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影作品非常自然地被各种形式的歧视所带来的影响卷入其中，无论朝着哪个方向。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "几个世纪以来，才能一直凌驾于对作者行为的观察之上。创作者不过是作品的一个附属：放荡的生活、性行为、政治反对意见、奢侈之风，甚至亵渎神明，只要其产出——无论是见证还是想象——能够被赞助人接受并有望流传后世，社会便会予以容忍。艺术家的行为或许会令人震惊、恼火、冒犯。但作品的后世影响力占了上风。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "近年来，作品已沦为附着于某种个性光环之上的可选配件。只要个人主义受到吹捧，产出便无足轻重。名气压倒了专业知识与创作。这种现象被一种反常效应加剧了：每个人都要求进入流行和对他们“自我”认可的封闭圈子。值得注意的是，这种效应被一些毫无节操的追名逐利者极大地放大了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是艺术史演变中的普遍现象，摄影也卷入其中。摄影尤其受到关注。因为表面上看，许多人认为创作一张摄影图像不需要多少专业知识。然而每个摄影师都知道，对于光线这一复杂工作不可或缺的众多工具，将其付诸实践可能是最困难、最令人筋疲力尽的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "评选标准不再取决于图像的意义，而是取决于其作者所持的立场。评选者因各种原因进行歧视。它始于各种形式的压力、微妙的敲诈，或是所谓艺术行政人员的随波逐流。我还记得那些在评选时甚至不关心作者是谁、为一张图像惊叹的摄影评委。最近，在拒绝匿名之后（并非所有人都能吸取先前的教训），一个评审团在甚至还没看到照片、听到作者作品宣布时就欣喜若狂。我们所有人都会拍出毫无兴致的照片；一些同僚惊讶地发现，他们的一些所谓的“垃圾”照片竟然成了投机倒把的对象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "基于消极歧视的评选有时会以往往多变且不可理解的标准排斥某些作者的作品。一个昨天还被抢购其图像的狂热群众所崇拜的摄影师，今天却成了一个被遗弃的人，其原因与他的作品毫无关系。一位曾经备受追捧肖像画的肖像摄影师，却因分享了一次政治观点而被“列入黑名单”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，为了对抗这些不可接受的行为，一些人发明了同样高度多变的积极歧视。图像的选择依据是将作者分类的参数，而这些参数与可能挂在画廊墙上的照片完全没有关系。公开宣称的立场、便利的裙带关系、经济利益、展示的风俗，都是展示“垃圾”不可避免的参数。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "总而言之：歧视在其所有方面在艺术中都没有容身之地，在摄影中更是如此。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "矛盾在于永久的时间动荡，它们一代又一代地改变着航向。时尚改变了图像和作者的评选标准。今天被谴责的风俗明天可能会受到崇拜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "歧视成功地在艺术界播下了地狱般的混乱，尽管它从根本上与此无关。显然，行政知识分子已经偷走了我们对每一个摄影图像创作特性的珍视，并将其糟蹋殆尽：即杰作（Œuvre）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此外，无论是实行消极歧视还是宣称积极歧视，所有歧视都令人痛恨！", I say mists out of modesty, for at times we shall run into fogs thick enough to obscure even the sharpest and most tolerant eyes. Drawing on various definitions, legal as well as literary, we can broadly understand “discrimination” to mean pushing away a person or an object because of belonging to a different community or way of life. The exclusion of all these communities, so different in their criteria of association, is broadly held to be forbidden by the Law and wholly unjustifiable in what is called collective social life. Rejecting an individual from society because of color, private life, philosophical references or sectarian opinions is utterly reprehensible. Yet it remains the case that equality of brainpower, of physical potential, of sensual assets, does not exist."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As is often the case, today’s problems were born of confusion. A crude blending of genres, between the desirable and the lived, drives us into a complete impasse that impairs creativity and competence."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Photographic works find themselves quite naturally caught up, in one direction or other, by the impact of the many forms of discrimination."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For centuries, talent prevailed over observations about authors’ behavior. The creator was an accessory to a body of work: dissolute lives, sexual conduct, political opposition, extravagances, even blasphemies were tolerated by societies as long as the output, whether testimony or imagination, was acceptable to patrons and promised to endure. The artist’s behavior might shock, irritate, offend. But the work’s posterity prevailed."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In recent years, works have become no more than an optional accessory attached to the aura of a personality. The output hardly matters so long as egos are adulated. Celebrity takes precedence over know-how and creation. The phenomenon is heightened by a perverse effect: everyone’s demand to gain entry to the closed circle of popularity and recognition of their “Me.” It is worth noting that this effect is greatly amplified by a few unscrupulous money-spinners."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is a generality in the evolution of the history of Art, in which photography is involved. Photography is particularly concerned. For, on the face of it, many people think that making a photographic image requires little particular knowledge. Yet every photographer knows that the many tools indispensable to the complex work with light are probably the most difficult and the most tiring to put into practice."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Selection criteria no longer rest on the significance of the images, but on the positions their authors take. Selectors discriminate for many reasons. It begins with pressure of every kind, subtle blackmail, or the herd-following of so-called artistic administrators. I remember those photographer jurors who marveled at an image without even caring who the author was during the selection. Recently, after refusing anonymity (not everyone is still able to learn the prior lesson), a jury went into raptures at the announcement of an author’s work, before even seeing the photographs. All of us commit photographs of no interest; some colleagues were stunned to see a few of their so-called “garbage” pictures become objects of speculation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Selections based on negative discrimination sometimes exclude the work of certain authors on criteria that are very often variable and incomprehensible. A photographer adored by crowds who snapped up his images yesterday has become an outcast today, for reasons having no connection with his work. A portraitist whose images were once adulated finds herself “blacklisted” for having shared a political opinion."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So, to counter these unacceptable behaviors, some have invented positive discrimination, likewise highly variable. Image selection rests on sorting authors according to parameters that have strictly nothing to do with the photographs that might be hung on gallery walls. Openly assumed positions, convenient cronyism, financial interests, displayed mores are all unavoidable parameters for putting up “rubbish.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a word, in a thousand: discrimination in all its aspects has no place in Art, and even less in Photography."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The paradox lies in the permanent temporal upheavals that change course from generation to generation. The mores decried today will probably be adored tomorrow."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Discrimination has managed to sow infernal chaos in artistic circles, even though it is not fundamentally concerned. Decidedly, the administrative intelligentsia has stolen from us, and spoiled for us, the specificity of every creative photographic image: the Œuvre."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Besides, whether it is practiced negatively or declared positive, all discrimination remains hateful!"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Thierry Maindrault – October 16, 2026"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Your comments on this column and its photograph are always welcome at [email protected]", "links": [{"text": "[email protected]", "url": "https://loeildelaphotographie.com/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#ef8c879d8081869e9a8a9caf828e86818b9d8e9a839bc18e9d9b"}]}]

Thierry Maindrault’s Monthly Cogitations

I am steering your reflection toward a topical subject, perfectly suited to the mists (autumnal or springlike, depending on your hemisphere) now rolling in. I say mists out of modesty, for at times we shall run into fogs thick enough to obscure even the sharpest and most tolerant eyes. Drawing on various definitions, legal as well as literary, we can broadly understand “discrimination” to mean pushing away a person or an object because of belonging to a different community or way of life. The exclusion of all these communities, so different in their criteria of association, is broadly held to be forbidden by the Law and wholly unjustifiable in what is called collective social life. Rejecting an individual from society because of color, private life, philosophical references or sectarian opinions is utterly reprehensible. Yet it remains the case that equality of brainpower, of physical potential, of sensual assets, does not exist.

As is often the case, today’s problems were born of confusion. A crude blending of genres, between the desirable and the lived, drives us into a complete impasse that impairs creativity and competence.

Photographic works find themselves quite naturally caught up, in one direction or other, by the impact of the many forms of discrimination.

For centuries, talent prevailed over observations about authors’ behavior. The creator was an accessory to a body of work: dissolute lives, sexual conduct, political opposition, extravagances, even blasphemies were tolerated by societies as long as the output, whether testimony or imagination, was acceptable to patrons and promised to endure. The artist’s behavior might shock, irritate, offend. But the work’s posterity prevailed.

In recent years, works have become no more than an optional accessory attached to the aura of a personality. The output hardly matters so long as egos are adulated. Celebrity takes precedence over know-how and creation. The phenomenon is heightened by a perverse effect: everyone’s demand to gain entry to the closed circle of popularity and recognition of their “Me.” It is worth noting that this effect is greatly amplified by a few unscrupulous money-spinners.

This is a generality in the evolution of the history of Art, in which photography is involved. Photography is particularly concerned. For, on the face of it, many people think that making a photographic image requires little particular knowledge. Yet every photographer knows that the many tools indispensable to the complex work with light are probably the most difficult and the most tiring to put into practice.

Selection criteria no longer rest on the significance of the images, but on the positions their authors take. Selectors discriminate for many reasons. It begins with pressure of every kind, subtle blackmail, or the herd-following of so-called artistic administrators. I remember those photographer jurors who marveled at an image without even caring who the author was during the selection. Recently, after refusing anonymity (not everyone is still able to learn the prior lesson), a jury went into raptures at the announcement of an author’s work, before even seeing the photographs. All of us commit photographs of no interest; some colleagues were stunned to see a few of their so-called “garbage” pictures become objects of speculation.

Selections based on negative discrimination sometimes exclude the work of certain authors on criteria that are very often variable and incomprehensible. A photographer adored by crowds who snapped up his images yesterday has become an outcast today, for reasons having no connection with his work. A portraitist whose images were once adulated finds herself “blacklisted” for having shared a political opinion.

So, to counter these unacceptable behaviors, some have invented positive discrimination, likewise highly variable. Image selection rests on sorting authors according to parameters that have strictly nothing to do with the photographs that might be hung on gallery walls. Openly assumed positions, convenient cronyism, financial interests, displayed mores are all unavoidable parameters for putting up “rubbish.”

In a word, in a thousand: discrimination in all its aspects has no place in Art, and even less in Photography.

The paradox lies in the permanent temporal upheavals that change course from generation to generation. Fashion alters the selection criteria for images and authors alike. The mores decried today will probably be adored tomorrow.

Discrimination has managed to sow infernal chaos in artistic circles, even though it is not fundamentally concerned. Decidedly, the administrative intelligentsia has stolen from us, and spoiled for us, the specificity of every creative photographic image: the Œuvre.

Besides, whether it is practiced negatively or declared positive, all discrimination remains hateful!

Thierry Maindrault – October 16, 2026

article_text:
Amid the hustle and bustle of Frieze London , where champagne bottles pop and deals are orchestrated, Brazilian abstract artist Marina Perez Simão wants to invite guests to contemplate inside a spaceship in Pace Gallery ’s booth. She’s painted 11 canvases in three main colors: three in blue, three in gray, and five in magenta.

The booth is arranged in the shape of the letter X, with two blue paintings on either side, a gray painting in the middle, and two others on the other side. Guests can either enter through the middle or on the sides.

“The structure is super open and closed at the same time, but there’s also a sense of discovery depending on which side you walk through,” Simão told ARTnews , speaking from São Paulo.

She wants viewers to take the paintings in and to get real close to her work. She describes the paintings as “more or less vague descriptions of strange worlds” and says that each artwork has its own “nature and behaviors.” “It’s abstract yet it has so many elements of landscape. Nature is a big, complex and vast organism that we don’t fully understand how it works, art is a way to approach these things that are difficult to explain,” Simão said.

Simão added that she wanted to remind her viewers that looking at art is a physical experience. “We see so many images through Instagram and digital platforms, which is fine, but we can’t forget that when you get close to a painting, there are different layers and textures,” she said, noting that she hopes people see the imperfections in her art—which is one of the reasons she doesn’t varnish her paintings.

When she started these paintings at the beginning of the year, she felt a natural development in her practice was taking place, but she found that it was still inexplicable.

Her paintings are often rich and bright in colors, with sky blues sitting atop grass green or bright reds paired with orange. These new works are cooler; they draw their inspiration from Pablo Picasso’s Blue and Rose Periods and Fra Angelico’s usage of the color pink.

“Pink is a difficult color because when you look at mass culture, there’s Barbie pink, bubblegum pink, and cotton candy pink. I didn’t want all these industrial pinks and their associations,” Simão said. She instead settled on magenta, given that it can be manipulated to mimic colors found in nature.

Simão found blue more challenging. She worked with the color straight from the tube because the pigment is already super strong, only occasionally relying on a dash of white for tinting. Yet she also combined different blues, mixing cobalt and cerulean, for example, to transform them into a greenish tone. The blue paintings “are almost impossible to photograph,” Simão explained. “We had to do three sessions of photographing as the pigments change so much.”

The gray paintings combine magenta and blue. In the first layers of the paintings, she hides hints of yellow and ocher, creating an effect similar to the hazy glow created when fog passes in front of the sun. According to Simão, the blue paintings are warm like summer, and the pink paintings are cold like winter. Together, they represent an abstract season.

Simão began experimenting with darker hues in 2024 with her exhibition “Solanaceae” at Pace in Los Angeles. The show’s name was inspired by the scientific name for the nightshades family of plants and the paintings had fragments of darkness. The same silhouette appeared in a show at Mendes Wood DM’s Paris gallery later that year. “I’ve been thinking about working with a limited color range [for a while] because color in my work is super important, and I wanted to study tonalities and limit myself, I’m always evolving,” said Simão.

Simão’s paintings at Frieze London changed her artistic routine. She hid everything in her studio that featured an ounce of color and resumed her usual position of painting away from the door and by a little terrace with a window.

“I paint standing up and in my socks. I don’t use chairs and sometimes I sit on the ground. These paintings required my body to be engaged,” said Simão.

article_text:
A previously unknown drawing by 18 th century Italian painter and printmaker Canaletto is heading to auction in England next week with an estimate of $53,000 to $79,000, after two centuries apparently spent in a single family’s collection.

The drawing, a fanciful architectural scene called a capriccio , will be on sale at Mallams auction house in Oxford on October 21. The work has been authenticated by Canaletto specialist Charles Beddington and dates to between 1746 and 1755, when the Venetian artist was working in England.

The pen and ink work shows a ruined Renaissance arcade, with vines and trees invading the crumbling stonework and a ramshackle wooden bridge that looks to be held together by wishful thinking as much as it is by rope. A boatman maneuvers his skiff out from under an archway. Broken wheels and wheels and dilapidated fences scatter the shore. Unlike the meticulously observed views of Venice and London for which Canaletto is most famous for, his capricci combined real and imaginary architecture to create scenes that never actually existed.

An inscription on the back could mean that Canaletto originally gave the drawing away as a gift. It was probably acquired in the late 18th century by Charles Burney, the English composer and music historian, and has remained with his descendants ever since.

The drawing may have been made as a preparatory study to show a prospective patron before Canaletto completed a related painting. That painting last appeared at Christie’s in London in 1995, when it sold for £380,000 (then $577,000), according to Artnet News .

Although Canaletto is most closely associated with his views of Venice’s canals and grand buildings, he began experimenting with capricci in the late 1730s. The genre gave him considerably more freedom to invent architectural settings, mixing classical ruins, waterways, and figures into elaborate imaginary landscapes.

Art historian John Rolfe told Artnet News that the works show Canaletto’s powers of observation as well as his imagination. He said the artist’s interest in the genre may have been influenced by a growing fascination with ruins, declining tourism in Venice during European wars, or his early experience working with his father, a theatrical set designer.

Canaletto’s market has produced some spectacular results recently. In July 2025, his Venice, the Return of the Bucintoro on Ascension Day sold for around $44 million at Christie’s London, setting an auction record for the artist. Another painting depicting the same Venetian ceremony fetched $30.5 million in February 2026.

His auction record for a capriccio stands at $3.3 million, achieved at Christie’s London in 1994.

The newly discovered drawing will be offered at a rather more accessible price, giving collectors a rare chance to acquire a work by one of Venice’s most celebrated painters.
